name: ARTAS robotic system
lead: The ARTAS system is a computer-assisted robotic device for hair restoration, made by Restoration Robotics and now marketed by Venus Concept. It uses image guidance to identify and extract individual follicular units from the donor scalp in follicular unit extraction (FUE), the technique that leaves small dot-like scars rather than a linear strip scar.[1][2][7]

People pursue it to restore hair density and a lower, fuller hairline: donor hairs taken from the back and sides of the scalp are moved to thinning areas, and transplanted hair is described as donor-dominant, meaning it keeps growing as it would have at its original site.[1] The robot automates the extraction step, which surgeons otherwise perform by hand with small punches.

Reference sources report US FDA clearance in 2011 for harvesting hair in men with brown or black hair, and describe a system using high-definition imaging and a dual-needle punch.[1][2] Reported drawbacks include higher cost than manual FUE, limits to FUE-style harvesting and the need for trained operators.[2] ClinicalTrials.gov lists manufacturer-associated studies comparing computer-assisted and manual harvest, but no results have been published.[3][4][5]
infobox: 2011, for harvesting in men with brown or black hair[1]
Not given; transplants are priced per graft, from about US$1.07 in Turkey to US$7.00 in Canada[1]

paras: According to a general reference, cameras map the donor area, and a dual-needle punch extracts follicular units; the cited punch depth is about 1 mm and the article cites transection rates under 5 percent and 400 to 800 grafts per hour.[2] Those numbers come from a reference page, not from trial data.

The manufacturer describes its current ARTAS iXi model as using a multi-camera stereoscopic vision system with stated 44-micron resolution, a seven-axis robotic arm and a proprietary punch, with touchscreen planning for the recipient area and the ability to create recipient sites and implant grafts in one platform; these are company claims.[7] The company also cites a 91 percent 'Worth It' rating on a patient review platform and states Health Canada licensing for harvesting follicles in men with black or brown straight hair.[7]

FUE generally uses 0.6 to 1.0 mm punches under local anaesthesia, takes under a week to recover from, needs no suture removal, and is described as longer and more costly than strip harvesting; Wikipedia notes patient candidacy is restricted.[1]

Wikipedia states the ARTAS system was approved by the FDA in 2011 for harvesting follicular units from men with brown or black hair.[1] Grokipedia describes the clearance as a 510(k) for men with androgenetic alopecia.[2]

Earlier milestones include Norman Orentreich's late-1950s work demonstrating donor dominance, and strip excision and stereo-microscopic dissection in the 1980s; NeoGraft received FDA approval in 2009 before ARTAS in 2011.[1]

Hair-loss discussion on T Nation has included the claim that the ARTAS machine has made hair transplantation easier, quicker and nearly undetectable, with a link to the manufacturer's product page.[8] Per Wikipedia's hair-transplantation history, techniques progressed from plugs and strip excision in the 20th century to follicular unit grafts, and robotic devices arrived after 2009.[1] Cost in the US, UK and Turkey varies widely by clinic and number of grafts.[1]

Grokipedia lists costs 20 to 40 percent above manual FUE and the need for specialised training.[2] A Canadian aesthetic surgery meeting abstract argued that most hair restoration candidates are not appropriate for FUE whether manual, NeoGraft-assisted or ARTAS robotic.[6]

No results have been published. Registered studies include a 2009 comparison of computer-assisted versus manual hair harvest (n=37),[3] a 2016 comparison of computer-assisted and manual implantation (n=32)[4] and a larger registered computer-assisted restoration study (n=150).[5]

timeline.event: Norman Orentreich transplants donor grafts for male pattern baldness and shows donor dominance.[1]
NeoGraft becomes the first FDA-approved robotic hair restoration device.[1]
FDA clearance of the ARTAS system for FUE harvesting.[1][2]
Registered studies of computer-assisted implantation begin.[4][5]

lore.intro: On forums, ARTAS is mentioned as technology that makes hair transplants more precise and less visible.[8]

claims.believers: A T Nation post describes the ARTAS machine as making transplantation easier, quicker and nearly undetectable.[8]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes FUE scars as small and 'virtually not visible'; no published results comparing ARTAS outcomes were found.[1][3]

card.summary: A FDA-cleared robot that harvests donor hairs for FUE; it automates extraction, and published outcome data were thin in the sources.
card.note: Reported to cost more than manual FUE; a surgeon abstract questions FUE candidacy generally.

quick.overview:
ARTAS is a robot from Restoration Robotics that finds and extracts donor hair follicles during FUE hair transplants. It was reported cleared by the FDA in 2011 for men.
It automates harvesting only; implantation still involves the surgical team. Registered trials compare it with manual harvest.
quick.mechanism: Imaging maps the donor scalp and a dual-needle punch extracts follicular units.
quick.risks: Risks are those of FUE generally. Reference sources note higher cost and training requirements; no trial results have been reported.

chain: Robot images the donor scalp and selects follicular units
Units are extracted with a small punch and transplanted
Permanent donor hair grows in thinning or receding areas
angle.text: Men with androgenetic alopecia who choose FUE use the robot for the harvesting step. Transplanted hair keeps its donor-area behaviour, so the result is added hair in the front or crown that continues to grow.
